metadata.title: Internet Number Registry and Routing Trust Residuality Stress Test
metadata.description: Explore how Internet number-resource and routing-trust services would need to change when sanctions separate an operator from its resources, cryptography underpinning RPKI must be replaced, measurement visibility becomes geographically biased, or a contested routing incident combines all three conditions.
metadata.naiveArchitecture: A member account holds registry resources and billing details, authorized users update registry and RPKI records, operators publish route authorizations, and public measurement systems observe routing and reachability. The design assumes the member, resource holder, operator, payer, authorized maintainer, cryptographic profile, and available measurement view change slowly and remain aligned.
metadata.residualArchitecture: The changed design separates resource rights, registry holder, sponsoring member, network operator, payer, contacts, jurisdictional restrictions, maintainer authority, cryptographic keys and algorithms, certificates, route objects, observations, vantage points, and published conclusions. Every authority and observation has scope and effective time, allowing custody continuity, cryptographic migration, and honest routing evidence even when organizations and network visibility fragment.
metadata.note: These tests focus on institutional and Internet-wide change, not a routine server failure. The key change is to stop treating one member account, one cryptographic chain, or one measurement view as the permanent source of truth.

source.title: Residues: Time, Change, and Uncertainty in Software Architecture
source.author: Barry M. O'Reilly

stressors.name: Sanctions and corporate collapse separate a network operator from the organization that holds its number resources
stressors.detection: Sanctions notices, court and registry filings, member and billing status, resource and maintainer records, operating contacts, transfer requests, network announcements, creditor claims, and legal review.
stressors.attractor: The legal holder, paying member, technical operator, authorized maintainer, and people keeping the network reachable are no longer one functioning organization. Freezing the account may strand legitimate routing operations; accepting informal changes may enable resource hijacking or evade legal restrictions.
stressors.businessReaction: Freeze prohibited financial and ownership actions, preserve safe technical continuity where legally allowed, verify control and claims through independent evidence, appoint accountable contacts or custodial arrangements, separate urgent operational updates from permanent transfer, and publish an auditable registry outcome.
stressors.residue: Separate number resource, registration right, legal holder, sponsoring member, payer, network operator, maintainer authority, technical contact, jurisdiction, restriction, temporary custody, operational change, ownership transfer, evidence, decision, and effective period. Each action evaluates the authority and legal scope it actually requires.

impacts.effect: Registry operation preserves legitimate network continuity without confusing technical control, membership, payment, and legal ownership.
Operators can reconcile or transfer resources through evidence appropriate to each right and restriction.
Readiness distinguishes legal title, registry sponsorship, technical operation, maintainer access, payment, and sanctions clearance.
First-pass acceptance measures whether each claimed authority has the right evidence, not whether one account appears complete.
Adds restricted-action handling, temporary custody, evidence-backed authority changes, continuity decisions, and effective-dated transfer.
Supports exceptional reconciliation without silently converting technical continuity into permanent ownership.
Models claims, approvals, conditions, effective dates, contested rights, and temporary arrangements separately.
Decouples member lifecycle and contractual status from the continuing registry state of number resources.
Scopes maintainer authority to specific resources, actions, evidence, restrictions, and time windows.
Owns continuity decisions with legal, member services, security, routing, policy, and affected network operators.
Makes institution-failure and jurisdiction-aware resource continuity a peer-registry benchmark.

stressors.name: A cryptographic breakthrough makes the algorithm protecting current RPKI certificates unsafe
stressors.detection: Standards and research disclosure, trust-anchor and certificate inventory, key age and custody, relying-party support, route-object coverage, operator readiness, test results, revocation state, and routing observations.
stressors.attractor: The trust system must move quickly, but issuers, operators, routers, and relying parties cannot all change at once. An immediate cutover invalidates legitimate routes; prolonged dual trust permits unsafe credentials; replacing certificates without preserving authorization history makes disputes impossible to explain.
stressors.businessReaction: Agree a migration policy, inventory affected objects, introduce algorithm-agile profiles, issue replacement chains, support bounded overlap, test relying parties, communicate operator actions, revoke unsafe material in waves, monitor routing effects, and preserve the lineage of every authorization.
stressors.residue: Separate resource authority, cryptographic profile, algorithm, trust anchor, certificate, key, custodian, route authorization intent, signed object, validity window, publication channel, relying-party capability, migration wave, revocation, and observed routing outcome. One authorization can be represented by multiple bounded cryptographic objects during migration.

impacts.effect: Routing security remains operable through a cryptographic transition rather than binding trust to one permanent algorithm.
Engineers can preserve intended route authorization while keys, certificates, and relying parties migrate.
Validity monitoring distinguishes authorization intent, old and new object chains, relying-party readiness, and route outcome.
Invalid announcements are segmented by unauthorized origin, migration mismatch, stale object, and relying-party capability.
Adds cryptographic profiles, migration waves, dual-object lineage, relying-party readiness, and controlled revocation.
Treats algorithm replacement as a governed ecosystem migration rather than an in-place key update.
Supports multiple approved cryptographic profiles and trust chains with explicit migration and retirement state.
Preserves route-authorization intent while issuing, validating, and retiring multiple signed representations.
Uses the same algorithm-agile authority and object lifecycle for emerging routing-security objects.
Owns migration with standards bodies, peer registries, operators, relying-party vendors, security teams, and communications.
Makes coordinated algorithm-agile RPKI migration a global registry-community benchmark.

stressors.name: Governments and network failures remove whole regions from the public measurement view
stressors.detection: Probe and collector reachability, geographic and network coverage, sampling changes, blocked protocols, cable and peering events, operator reports, route collectors, independent datasets, and analyst review.
stressors.attractor: Dashboards still produce precise-looking regional and global conclusions while the remaining probes and collectors overrepresent reachable networks. Missing observations are mistaken for normal operation, policy debates use biased evidence, and downstream API consumers cannot tell that the meaning of a metric changed.
stressors.businessReaction: Declare coverage loss, separate observed absence from confirmed failure, estimate which populations and networks are no longer represented, use alternative sources and operator-submitted evidence, restrict claims, publish caveats and revisions, and help integrators react to changing fitness.
stressors.residue: Separate measurement question, method, requested population, vantage point, network and geography, collection path, observation window, availability, sample weight, raw observation, enrichment, derived metric, coverage assessment, conclusion, caveat, revision, and downstream release. Every published result carries the scope it can support.

impacts.effect: Researchers receive evidence whose geographic and network limits remain visible when the observable Internet shrinks.
Analysts can distinguish reachability change from measurement blind spots and explain what conclusions remain supported.
Collection records coverage, path, population, loss, alternative evidence, and comparability before enrichment.
Vantage-point adequacy is evaluated for the question and population, not as a raw probe count.
Adds coverage health, representativeness, restricted conclusions, revision notices, and downstream fitness metadata.
Combines control-plane, data-plane, operator, and independent evidence without hiding blind spots.
Versions probe eligibility, availability, network and geographic coverage, and measurement-path constraints.
Publishes collector and peer coverage changes alongside routing observations and derived events.
Attaches method, population, coverage, caveats, revisions, and compatibility to every dataset release.
Owns evidence fitness with probe hosts, collectors, operators, researchers, policy teams, and API consumers.
Makes transparent measurement coverage and Internet-state inference a public-data benchmark.

stressors.name: Contested resources announce new origins during the cryptographic migration while regional measurements are dark
stressors.detection: Registry rights and restrictions, temporary operator authority, old and new RPKI objects, relying-party readiness, BGP collectors, reachable probes, missing-region coverage, operator-submitted traces, traffic reports, and incident communications.
stressors.attractor: The announcements may be a hijack, an authorized continuity action, a stale cryptographic object, or an artifact of partial visibility. Automatically accepting or rejecting them can disconnect users or legitimize misuse, and the organization cannot rely on one account, one validation state, or one global-looking chart.
stressors.businessReaction: Establish current operational and legal authority, compare intended authorizations across both cryptographic profiles, state measurement gaps, gather independent operator evidence, publish bounded conclusions, coordinate corrective objects or route action, and preserve the incident and policy decisions for review.
stressors.residue: No new structural change is required: scoped resource authority explains who may act, algorithm-agile authorization preserves intent across old and new certificates, and coverage-aware measurements distinguish observed routing from blind regions. One incident record composes the existing evidence and decisions.

impacts.effect: Policy participants can review a contested incident using explicit authority, cryptographic, and measurement uncertainty.
Public-interest discussion receives a defensible regional account without overclaiming what dark networks reveal.
The explanation separates registry authority, RPKI intent, validation compatibility, observed routes, missing coverage, and remaining questions.
Explainability includes the evidence scope and competing interpretations behind a routing-policy conclusion.
Publishes an accessible incident and policy record linked to technical evidence, decisions, revisions, and implementation.
Reuses the existing authority, migration, and measurement residues as evidence for community review.
Shows the effective registry holder, operator, maintainer, restrictions, and disputed or temporary state.
Composes registry, RPKI, BGP, measurement coverage, and operator evidence with visible caveats.
Records the proposal, incident evidence, community discussion, decision, implementation, and later revision.
Coordinates registry, routing, measurement, legal, member, policy, communications, and affected-operator work.
Makes transparent compound routing-incident governance central to the registry's own public-trust standard.
